title: The mood of a raga
hookLine: each hymn of the Granth is set in a raga, a musical mood for the words

lines: THE MUSIC TELLS YOU THE SCENE.
A SCRIPTURE WITH MOODS BUILT IN.
cards: A few low notes, and you know something's wrong. A bright little tune, and it's morning and everyone's fine. Movie composers know this: before a single word is spoken, the music tells you what kind of scene it is.
Play different music under the same line of dialogue, and it means something else. Now imagine a book of scripture where every hymn comes with that instruction built in.
Not just the words, but the mood they should be sung in. That's how the Guru Granth Sahib is organized, and it's today's word.

teach.b: Raag. In English you'll often see it spelled raga. It's a musical framework from Indian classical music: a set of notes, a shape of melody, and above all a mood.
The Guru Granth Sahib is divided by raag.

teach.h: THIRTY-ONE RAAGS, EACH IN ITS HEADING.
teach.b: After the opening prayers, the hymns are grouped into sections, thirty-one main raags, and every hymn carries its raag in its heading. Open almost any page, and the first thing written above a shabad is its musical mood.
Each raag has a feeling, and many have a time of day or a season. Basant is spring, bright and fresh. Malhar is the monsoon, when rain breaks a long heat.

Some are for dawn, some for evening, some carry longing, some peace. The Gurus chose them on purpose, so the music would carry the meaning of the words, not fight it. The first raag in the Granth is Sri Raag.
Guru Amar Das says of it, in paraphrase, that among the raags Sri Raag is the best, but only if through it you come to love the True One. That's how the Gurus saw music.
The raag serves the Word; it's the vehicle, not the point.
Sung in its raag, kirtan lets the listener feel the mood before understanding a single word.
This week had the same shape: tan seva, the purse and the mind, haumai, seva, kirtan, and now raag, the teaching carried into the body, the wallet, the voice and the ear.

how: Each shabad in the Guru Granth Sahib is headed with its raag, and trained kirtan musicians sing it in that raag; some gurdwaras and schools work to keep the traditional raag settings alive.

o: a chapter of the Granth gathered by its author
a prayer recited without any music, at dawn
a musical mood that a hymn is set to be sung in

games.q: you're setting a hymn about the monsoon breaking a long drought. which raag fits its mood?
o: any raag at all; the mood doesn't matter.
games.why: Malhar is the raag of the rains. the Gurus chose raags so the music would carry the meaning of the words.

practice: Play one song or shabad, or remember one you know well, and before you think about the words, ask: what's the mood? Morning or night, longing or peace, heavy or light?
Don't name it too fast; let the feeling show up in your body first, in your chest, your shoulders, your breath, and then notice how it shapes the words.

wordCard.voice: Raag. A musical mood, and the way the Guru Granth Sahib is ordered, so each hymn is sung in a feeling that fits its words. Your week: hands, purse, mind, haumai, seva, kirtan, and raag.
